summary: Defines an SMTP extension whereby a server says it can accept several commands in a single TCP send, so the client does not wait for a reply after each one. It is a standards-track document, later replaced by RFC 2197.

eli5.summary: Instead of asking one question and waiting, you hand over a list of questions and get all the answers.

questions: how does pipelining speed up email
why do some smtp servers not support pipelining
subtitle: Send multiple email commands at once instead of waiting for each reply.

tldr.problem: SMTP forces clients to send one command and wait for a server response before sending the next command, causing delays on high-latency network links.
tldr.mechanism: The PIPELINING extension lets clients batch multiple commands into a single network send, so the server processes them all and sends all responses back together.
tldr.outcome: Email sending becomes significantly faster, especially over slow links. Some servers cannot handle this and will lose or drop pipelined commands, so clients must check for the PIPELINING capability before using it.

facts.label: Commands that can be pipelined
facts.value: RSET, MAIL FROM, SEND FROM, SOML FROM, SAML FROM, RCPT TO

facts.label: Commands that must end a group
facts.value: EHLO, DATA, VRFY, EXPN, TURN, QUIT, NOOP

today: RFC 1854 was replaced by RFC 2197, which consolidated SMTP service extensions. Pipelining is now widely supported in modern SMTP servers and is a standard way to improve mail transmission performance.

sections.title: The Problem with One Command at a Time
sections.content:
The original SMTP protocol (RFC 821) has a simple structure: the client sends one command, the server sends one response, then the client sends the next command. On network links with high latency—the delay for a message to reach the other end and come back—this is inefficient. The client spends most of its time waiting for responses instead of sending the next command.

Some SMTP servers have bugs that make them lose or corrupt pipelined commands even though the RFC does not forbid them, so clients cannot safely use this optimization without confirmation.
sections.eli5: Imagine you can only ask one question, get an answer, then ask the next question. On a slow connection this takes forever.

sections.title: The PIPELINING Extension
sections.content:
RFC 1854 defines a simple way for clients to check whether a server supports pipelining. When the client opens a connection and sends EHLO instead of the older HELO command, the server responds with a list of capabilities. If pipelining is supported, the response includes the keyword PIPELINING.

If the client sees PIPELINING in the response, it knows it can batch commands. No new commands or parameters are needed—the extension is purely about allowing existing commands to be sent in groups.
sections.eli5: The server tells you 'I can handle pipelining' using one special keyword in its greeting. That is all you need to know.

sections.title: How Clients and Servers Use Pipelining
sections.content:
Once a client confirms the server supports PIPELINING, it can send groups of commands without waiting for responses. Some commands such as RSET, MAIL FROM, and RCPT TO can appear anywhere in a pipelined group. Others like DATA, QUIT, EHLO, and VRFY must be the last command in a group because they change the state of the connection.

The client must carefully track all responses received and match them to the commands sent. If some RCPT TO commands are rejected but DATA is accepted, the client must send the message and then decide what to do next—it cannot assume DATA will fail just because some recipients failed.

Servers that support pipelining must never lose buffered commands, must process groups correctly, and should buffer responses to commands that do not change state so they can be sent as a unit.
sections.eli5: You send a batch of commands, get all the answers back, and check each answer carefully. It is faster, but you have to be careful to understand all the replies.

sections.title: Performance Improvement
sections.content:
In the RFC's example, a simple mail delivery without pipelining takes 9 round-trip exchanges: greeting, HELO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO (three times), DATA, message content, and QUIT. With pipelining, the same task takes only 4 round trips. On a link with 100 milliseconds of latency in each direction, this saves 500 milliseconds.

The benefit grows with more recipients and longer network delays. The RFC notes that some non-trivial number of Internet SMTP servers cannot handle pipelined commands at all, which is why checking for the PIPELINING capability is essential.
sections.eli5: If each exchange takes a quarter second, the old way takes 2.25 seconds. Pipelining cuts it to half a second for the same work.
